standard.title: Evidence changes knowledge
standard.description: explain how new evidence or different perspectives can lead to changes in scientific knowledge
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can examine why scientific advances depend on collaboration and building on prior work (AC9S5H01). They have not yet explained how specific new evidence or perspectives cause established scientific knowledge to change.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain how new evidence or different perspectives can lead to changes in scientific knowledge.

nodes.label: Scientific knowledge is based on evidence
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify that scientific knowledge is built from evidence and that the type and quality of evidence matters
nodes.minimum_width: State that scientific knowledge is based on evidence; give one example of evidence that supports a scientific idea
nodes.typical_width: Distinguish between types of evidence (observational, experimental, technological) and explain why some evidence is more convincing than others
wider: Investigate how First Nations Australians' ecological observations constitute evidence that informs scientific understanding
Compare evidence from different fields (e.g. fossil record vs DNA analysis) that supports the same scientific idea
Research how al-Battani's astronomical calculations provided new evidence that refined earlier models of the solar year

response_modes.reason: Students need to accumulate a range of evidence types and examples — observational, experimental, technological, cultural — before they can reason about what makes evidence convincing or how it drives change. A single example of evidence is not enough to generalise the concept; breadth of examples builds the repertoire needed for Node 2.

success_criteria: States that scientific knowledge is based on evidence
Gives one correct example of evidence supporting a scientific idea
Does not confuse evidence with opinion or belief

nodes.label: New evidence changes scientific understanding
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how new evidence — from new technology, methods or discoveries — has led to changes in scientific understanding
nodes.minimum_width: Identify one example of how scientific understanding has changed over time as new evidence or methods became available; explain what changed and why
nodes.typical_width: Investigate how scientific understanding in at least two content areas has developed through new evidence or technology; explain the role of evidence in each case
wider: Explore how scientists are re-examining organism relationships using new genetic evidence to refine classification
Investigate how aeronautical engineers' evolving understanding of forces in flight led to changes in aircraft design
Research how improvements in microscopy led to changes in biological classification systems

response_modes.reason: Students commonly treat changed scientific knowledge as a sign of unreliability rather than a feature of the evidence-based process. Seeing multiple examples across different content areas (classification, astronomy, forces) helps students recognise the pattern — that change is how science works, not a flaw. Single-example teaching reinforces the misconception; breadth resolves it.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The wider array spans genuinely different knowledge domains — biology (classification via genetics), engineering (aircraft design), astronomy (al-Battani) — each illustrating a different mechanism by which new evidence drives change. Advancing students who engage multiple domains develop a transferable explanatory framework rather than a context-specific example.
success_criteria: Names a specific example where scientific understanding changed due to new evidence
Explains what the new evidence was and how it caused the change
Does not describe the change as science being 'wrong before'

nodes.label: Different perspectives shape knowledge
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how different perspectives — including cultural, historical and disciplinary — contribute to the development of scientific knowledge
nodes.minimum_width: Identify one example where a different perspective contributed new understanding to a scientific field; explain the contribution
nodes.typical_width: Compare how two different perspectives (e.g. First Nations ecological knowledge and Western ecology) approach the same phenomenon; explain what each contributes
wider: Investigate how First Nations Australians' land management practices inform contemporary environmental management to protect biodiversity
Investigate how First Nations Australians' traditional ecological knowledges inform sustainable harvesting practices of species such as dugongs and turtles
Research how perspectives from different scientific disciplines (e.g. genetics and palaeontology) together changed understanding of a phenomenon

response_modes.reason: Students commonly name a different perspective without explaining the contribution — they describe the perspective rather than reasoning through what it adds to scientific knowledge. Scaffolding the reasoning explicitly (what did this perspective see that others missed, and what did science gain from including it?) is what moves students from description to explanation.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The First Nations ecological knowledge directions here are genuinely rich — sustainable harvesting, land management, biodiversity protection — and connect to real contemporary scientific practice. Advancing students who investigate these cases develop a nuanced understanding of how non-Western knowledge systems contribute distinct insights, not just parallel versions of Western science.
success_criteria: Names a specific example where a different perspective contributed to scientific knowledge
Explains the contribution rather than just naming the perspective
Recognises that multiple perspectives can coexist and contribute to understanding

nodes.label: Evidence and perspectives together refine knowledge
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how the interplay of new evidence and different perspectives leads to ongoing refinement of scientific knowledge
nodes.minimum_width: Explain how both new evidence and different perspectives contributed to a change in scientific knowledge in one case; identify that this process is ongoing
nodes.typical_width: Construct an explanation tracing how a specific area of scientific knowledge (e.g. classification, astronomy) has been refined through multiple rounds of new evidence and perspective shifts
wider: Evaluate whether a specific change in scientific knowledge was driven primarily by new evidence, new perspectives, or both — justify with examples
Investigate a current area where scientific knowledge is being refined by new evidence or perspectives and explain what is changing and why
Compare two cases of knowledge change — one driven primarily by technology (new evidence) and one driven primarily by cultural perspective — and explain what each reveals about how science works

response_modes.reason: This node brings together the evidence strand (Node 2) and the perspectives strand (Node 3) into a coordinated explanation of knowledge refinement. Students who can explain each separately but cannot articulate their interplay have not met the descriptor's full demand — the integration of both into a coherent account of how science develops is the learning.

The evaluative tasks in the wider tier — judging whether a change was driven by evidence or perspective, or both — require explicit reasoning scaffolding. Students need to be supported in constructing the argument structure: claim, evidence strand, perspective strand, and how they interact. Without this scaffold, students produce description rather than evaluation.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The comparative direction — contrasting technology-driven and perspective-driven knowledge change — gives advancing students a genuine analytical lens for understanding how science develops. This is rich beyond the minimum because it asks students to theorise about the mechanisms of scientific change, not just describe instances of it.
success_criteria: Explains how both new evidence and different perspectives contributed to a knowledge change
Identifies that scientific knowledge refinement is an ongoing process
